claims.text: Conventional eutectic high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloys usually have straight lamellar or rod-like eutectic morphologies.
Phase-field simulation can reveal how a kinked or vermicular eutectic microstructure forms.
Coupling comprehensive free-energy sampling, phase-field simulation, and ab initio inputs can accurately predict processing windows for producing kinked or vermicular eutectic microstructures.
Tuning cooling rate and localized compositional fluctuations according to the model will promote a kinked or vermicular eutectic morphology.
A vermicular eutectic morphology introduces additional phase boundaries in multiple orientations.
The additional, multidirectionally oriented phase boundaries pin dislocations.
The additional phase boundaries arrest crack propagation.
Straight eutectic morphologies arise from preferred crystallographic locking associated with interphase anisotropy during solidification.
A lack or disruption of crystallographic locking permits formation of the kinked eutectic morphology.
Comprehensive free-energy sampling identifies the specific processing conditions that disrupt crystallographic locking.
The vermicular morphology enables the soft FCC phase to bear more deformation and better exploits the strain-hardening capacity of the constituent phases.
The guided vermicular microstructure will produce a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to straight-morphology controls.
The guided vermicular microstructure will produce a statistically significant increase in ductility relative to straight-morphology controls.
The guided vermicular microstructure will produce a statistically significant increase in Young's modulus relative to straight-morphology controls.
The guided vermicular microstructure will produce a statistically significant increase in fracture toughness or fracture resistance relative to straight-morphology controls.
The morphology subtly tunes the elastic response responsible for Young's modulus.
The proposed benefit should be evaluated at room temperature under moderate-to-high loads where elastic and plastic deformation are both active.
The methodology is valid only within a processing window that maintains phase and microstructural stability.
The methodology may remain effective at elevated temperatures if the designed microstructure remains stable.
Large deviations from modeled composition or processing conditions, or service conditions that destabilize the microstructure, may eliminate the expected improvements.
